profile.summary: LiPP, the Lipid-Protein Poses benchmark, asks a docking or cofolding tool to place a lipid in its binding site on a protein and scores the pose against the crystal structure. The set holds 331 nonredundant buried, or nonannular, lipid-protein complexes filtered out of BioDolphin version 1.1, all X-ray structures better than 2 Angstrom, covering the eight LIPID MAPS lipid classes and a range of protein functions. Within it, the 36 complexes released after 1 October 2021 form a test set that postdates the training or calibration cutoff of every tool the paper evaluates. Success is a lipid pose whose symmetry-corrected all-atom RMSD is below a cutoff, with a stricter criterion that also requires the pose to pass the PoseBusters physical checks. It is the set to use when choosing a tool for lipid-protein modelling, where small-molecule benchmarks do not apply.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a tool can reproduce the pose of a lipid bound inside a protein pocket. The authors restrict the question to nonannular interactions, meaning lipids held in buried or partly buried pockets as biological ligands, and leave out annular lipids that form a nonspecific shell around a membrane protein. Their reason for building the set is that lipid-protein modelling has no benchmark of its own: the available sets, such as the PoseBusters Benchmark and PDBbind, cover drug-like small molecules, and PDBbind's drug-likeness filter excludes many lipids because of their long aliphatic chains. A second question runs through the evaluation: whether the poses a tool produces are physically plausible at all, which is scored separately from how close they are to the crystal pose.

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The starting pool is BioDolphin version 1.1, 127,359 PDB entries each holding one lipid-protein pair. The filters follow the PoseBusters Benchmark recipe: keep X-ray structures better than 2 Angstrom; drop entries with unknown atom types or nonstandard residues, lipids that fail RDKit sanitisation, incomplete entries, and lipids covalently bonded to the protein; drop complexes whose PDB ligand report shows stereochemical errors or atomic clashes; require the minimum lipid to protein distance to lie between 0.2 and 5 Angstrom; and drop entries where the lipid sits within 5 Angstrom of a protein symmetry mate. Redundancy is removed by clustering proteins at 90 per cent sequence identity with DIAMOND and keeping one randomly chosen pair per protein cluster and lipid Chemical Component Dictionary code. The remaining entries were curated by hand against the PDB structures and their papers. What is left is 331 pairs, with 235 unique lipids, lipid molecular weights from 88 to 1,229 Da and protein lengths from 107 to 856 residues. The split is by release date: 36 structures released after 1 October 2021 form the test set and the other 295 the precutoff set. Similarity between the two is assessed with ProteinCartography structure clustering and RDKit atom-pair Tanimoto similarity for the lipids.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: A submission is a modelled complex per benchmark entry, and the five tools evaluated are given different inputs by design. The cofolding tools AlphaFold 3, Chai-1 and RoseTTAFold AA get a protein sequence and a lipid identifier, a SMILES string or a CCD code. The docking tools AutoDock Vina and DiffDock-L get the experimental coordinates of protein and lipid and have to place the lipid; Vina is given pocket positions inferred from the experimental complex while DiffDock-L is run without pocket information. All tools are run with default parameters and no post-prediction refinement, and one top pose per complex is kept, chosen by that tool's own score. Cofolded complexes are superimposed on the experimental structure through the protein coordinates before measurement, which is unnecessary for the docking tools because they were given the experimental protein. The lipid pose error is the symmetry-corrected RMSD computed with spyRMSD. Success is the percentage of complexes under a cutoff, reported from 2 to 3 Angstrom, and the stricter criterion also requires the model to pass every PoseBusters category, which the paper calls PB-valid. Success rates are reported with 95 per cent confidence intervals from the exact binomial distribution, and are broken down by lipid molecular weight and lipid class. A separate analysis asks how well each tool's own confidence score predicts its error, using ipTM for AlphaFold 3 and Chai-1, inter-PAE for RoseTTAFold AA, the confidence score for DiffDock-L and the affinity score for AutoDock Vina.

These are protein and small-molecule sets, not lipid data, and the paper states that the values in those columns were taken from the literature rather than measured here. Several cells are empty because a tool has not been evaluated on PoseBusters, and the AlphaFold 3 column carries a footnote that the published rates used a 2019-09-30 training cutoff. sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The sets and the reproduction code are in the mcshanlab/LiPP_Benchmark repository. The data folder holds the general set, the test set and a small example set as CSV tables of BioDolphin identifiers with metadata, plus PDB files for each complex and for the protein and lipid split apart. To reproduce the published benchmark a user installs whichever of the five tools they want to test, along with OpenStructure and ProteinCartography, records the paths in config.yaml, and downloads the BioDolphin version 1.1 table into the data folder. Each tool has its own folder under scripts/run_tools with a README: for AlphaFold 3 it is three conda environments, a preprocessing script, a run.sh meant to be submitted to a cluster scheduler, a PyMOL superposition step, an OpenStructure scoring step and a summarising script. The analysis folder holds the evaluation, whose compare.py reads one concatenated table of lipid and protein errors for all methods and produces the success rates and figures.

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: A time split, and no training split. The benchmark is evaluation only: the 331 complexes are divided by PDB release date into the 36-complex test set released after 1 October 2021 and the 295-complex precutoff set, because 1 October 2021 is the day after the latest training or calibration cutoff among the five tools evaluated. The paper reports results on the full 331 and on the 36 separately.

quotes.text: The LiPP benchmark set can be separated into two subsets: a test set consisting of PDB structures released after the cutoff date and a precutoff set consisting of structures released before the cutoff.
These complexes were designated as the LiPP test set to evaluate method performance on unseen data (defined as data not explicitly used for training/calibration).

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Success rate, higher is better, under two criteria. The first is the percentage of complexes whose lipid pose has a symmetry-corrected all-atom RMSD below a cutoff, reported from 2 to 3 Angstrom, with 2 Angstrom used in Table 2. The second, in Table 3, additionally requires the model to pass every PoseBusters category, that is to be PB-valid. Success is also broken down by lipid class and molecular weight. Separately, each tool's own confidence score is compared against its RMSD to judge scoring power, and protein structure error is reported as TM-score and RMSD from OpenStructure.

quotes.text: Prediction success rates were defined as the percentage of cases with lipid RMSD values below a specified cutoff (ranging from 2 to 3 Å) for each method.
In a more stringent definition, successful predictions were additionally required to satisfy physical validity criteria (PB-valid) beyond the RMSD threshold.
we calculated the TM-score and the RMSD score between the experimental and modeled protein structures using the ost compare-structures command from OpenStructure version 2.11.1

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Five tools, run by the authors: three cofolding tools, AlphaFold 3 version 3.0.0, Chai-1 version 0.2.0 and RoseTTAFold All-Atom at commit 6c85140; one deep learning docking tool, DiffDock-L version 1.1.3; and one physics-based docking tool, AutoDock Vina version 1.2.3. The paper reports AlphaFold 3 as the best on the full set at 76.1 per cent under the 2 Angstrom criterion, falling to 47.2 per cent on the test set.

quotes.text: we systematically evaluate the performance of three AI-based cofolding tools (AlphaFold 3, Chai-1, RoseTTAFold AA), one AI-based docking tool (DiffDock-L), and one physics-based docking tool (AutoDock Vina)
AlphaFold 3 demonstrates the highest success rate at 76.1% under the RMSD < 2 Å criterion; however, the success rate drops to 47.2% for structures not seen during training.
Chai-1 version 0.2.0 was installed as a Python package

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Two. A redundancy filter at the set level: proteins are clustered at 90 per cent sequence identity with DIAMOND and only one pair is kept per cluster and lipid code, so near-identical complexes do not inflate the set. And a time split for training overlap: the 36-complex test set contains only structures released after the latest training or calibration cutoff of the five tools, which the paper lists per tool in Table 1. The authors also compare the test set and the precutoff set for protein structure and lipid chemical similarity rather than assuming the two are alike.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Curation of the LiPP Benchmark Set, Curation of the LiPP Test Set, Protein Similarity, Lipid Similarity

quotes.text: Within each protein cluster, if multiple proteins were complexed with the same lipid (identical Chemical Component Dictionary (CCD) ID code), we retained a single randomly chosen lipid–protein pair to avoid over-representation.
Structures present in the LiPP test set were not used for training of AlphaFold 3, Chai-1, RoseTTAFold AA, DiffDock-L, or AutoDock Vina.
we analyzed the similarity of lipid–protein pairs across the two sets from the perspective of both the protein and lipid molecules as described below

facts.label: Uncertainty
facts.value: 95 per cent confidence intervals on every success rate, calculated from the exact binomial distribution and printed in brackets beside each value. Sampling inside the tools is fixed rather than repeated: AlphaFold 3 used a single random seed with five diffusion samples, Chai-1 a single seed with five samples, RoseTTAFold AA one structure per sample, DiffDock-L ten poses and AutoDock Vina nine poses with no fixed random seed. One top pose per complex is carried into the scoring.

facts.value: One experimental lipid-protein complex structure, that is one lipid bound in one protein pocket, identified by a BioDolphin identifier. A model's lipid pose in that complex is what gets scored.

facts.value: Not stated as such. The entries are PDB crystal structures selected for resolution and quality, and the paper characterises them by protein functional class, including enzymes, immunological receptors, membrane proteins, signalling receptors and lipid transport proteins, rather than by species.

facts.label: Allowed inputs
facts.value: It depends on the tool class, and the paper is explicit that the two classes are not given the same information. Cofolding tools receive the protein sequence and a lipid SMILES string or CCD code only. Docking tools receive the experimental protein and lipid coordinates; AutoDock Vina is additionally given a pocket inferred from the experimental complex, DiffDock-L is not. RoseTTAFold AA additionally used multiple sequence alignments of up to 1024 sequences and up to four structural templates under its default configuration.

facts.label: Adaptation
facts.value: Out of the box, with no fine-tuning. Every tool was run at its released version with default parameters and settings, and no refinement was applied to its output. The authors note that a curated lipid-protein set could be used for fine-tuning docking force fields or cofolding weights, but that is proposed as future use and not done here.

outputs: Per-complex lipid and protein errors from the per-tool summarise step, and from compare.py the success rates, visualisations and a results report comparing the five methods, as its README describes them.
limitations: These commands were read from the paper and the repository and have not been executed by Rewire.
The run step for each tool is written for a cluster scheduler, and the tools themselves have to be installed and licensed separately.
PoseBusters validity and the Tanimoto and ProteinCartography similarity analyses live in other folders under scripts/analyze that were not opened here.

compare.py expects unique_rmsd.csv in its own directory and also reads ../PDB_Classifications/pdb_metadata.csv, and it writes unique_new_rmsd.csv for the subset released after the cutoff date; the saved files do not name any other input table.

notes: Numbers worth a human look. The abstract of the paper says LiPP is 'a curated data set of 311 nonredundant nonannular lipid-protein complex structures', while the Materials and Methods ('contains 331 lipid-protein pairs'), the Results, the headers of Tables 2 and 3 (N = 331) and the arithmetic 36 plus 295 all say 331. The repository's general_set.csv has 331 data rows, counted in this pass, and its README describes a pdb_structures_complex folder of native complex structures without giving a count, so 331 is used throughout this page and the abstract's 311 looks like an error in the source. The PoseBusters v1 and v2 columns are small-molecule results taken from other publications, not lipid data measured here; they are kept as structured entries because the store holds protocols for them, with their own set sizes of 428 and 308 and a note in the dataset field. Table 3 leaves the PoseBusters v1 column empty for every tool and prints one PoseBusters v2 value, 58 per cent for AutoDock Vina, with the other four tools shown as not evaluated. No licence is stated for the mcshanlab/LiPP_Benchmark repository in the GitHub metadata read here, so the data and code licence fields are null; the paper itself is CC BY 4.0. The record's existing source is the Europe PMC fullTextXML address, which has been failing with HTTP 500 for this run; the same full text was taken from NCBI E-utilities.
